history.intro: The life of Yitzhak "Jacques" Rosner unfolded within one of the most turbulent chapters in the history of East European Jewry. He was born in Iași in 1926, grew up in the village of Moldovița in southern Bukovina, was deported in 1941 to the Shargorod ghetto in Transnistria, survived, and made aliyah to Israel in 1968. This chapter describes the historical background of his life and of the lives of his parents, Litman and Regina. Every paragraph relies on sources listed at the end of the section, and every place where the history meets the family story is marked and linked to the stories Yitzhak wrote himself.

bio.1: Yitzhak "Jacques" Rosner was born on 25 November 1926 in Iași, Romania, the son of Litman and Regina (Gina) Rosner and the younger brother of Nelly. He grew up in the village of Moldovița in Bukovina, where some 400 to 500 Jews lived. His father worked in timber and exported it mainly to Britain and in part also to the Land of Israel, and from 1937 or 1938 he headed the Jewish committee in the village. As a boy Jacques played on the “Maccabi Moldovița” team, and thanks to Leo Schnap, a friend of the family, he was regarded among his friends as “the clever one” who knew things other children did not.
bio.2: In the summer of 1940 Jews were forbidden to live in villages, and the family moved to Gura Humorului. On 9 October 1941 they were deported with all the Jews of the town to Transnistria, and they reached the Shargorod ghetto. There, in one room that the four of them shared, they spent nearly three years of hunger, disease and forced labor. In the ghetto he hauled water from a distant spring and peeled potatoes in the gendarmerie kitchen. In those years he also taught himself Russian, with a grammar and a dictionary.
bio.3: After the Red Army liberated the ghetto in 1944, the family travelled via Czernowitz to Botoșani. There he was taken on as an interpreter at the Russian headquarters, and between July and October 1944 he served as a translator with the Second Ukrainian Front. According to a letter he wrote in 1991, from October 1944 to November 1948 he worked in Bucharest in the printing and distribution of the newspaper “România Liberă”, while completing secondary school in evening courses; his baccalaureate diploma was issued in March 1947. He studied electrical and radio engineering while working before dawn in the newspaper’s dispatch department, and in 1949 interrupted his studies to work as a radio technician at a state office. At the ELECTRONICA factory he helped a French team set up a television assembly line in the summer of 1960, and from 1963 until his aliyah he worked as a television technician in a repair laboratory. He was also certified as a translator from German, French and English into Romanian. In Bucharest he married Berta (Becca), and in 1954 their son Dan (Nicolai) was born there. The family album says that in the 1950s he “had to part with a senior post”, and that his parents and sister received visas to emigrate while he was left behind “despite 7–8 applications”.
bio.4: In 1968 he left Romania under the name “Adrian Roșca”, with a travel document for a person without citizenship. He passed through Vienna and landed at Lod on 15 May 1968. On 4 August 1968 he officially changed his name to Yitzhak Rosner, and on the same certificate his son Nicolai’s name was changed to Dan. In the autumn of 1968 he travelled to Canada and the United States. From 1970 to 1975 he headed the electrical department of Netivei Neft at the Abu Rudeis oil field in Sinai, and there he met Ruth – according to the family album, in August 1972. In March 1973 he divorced Berta, and on 12 April 1973 Yitzhak and Ruth were married in Tel Aviv. During the Yom Kippur War he guarded the field’s installations, and the field manager thanked him for the “hard time” they had gone through together. Sharon was born in March 1974 and Eylon in March 1975. As he wrote: “everything that happened after that is history that everyone knows.”
bio.5: In 1976 he received an Israeli citizenship certificate. In 1992 he attended an ABB course, and in January 1998 he received a certificate of recognition for his contribution to achieving “Operational Readiness” at Intel’s Fab 18 plant in Kiryat Gat. In his later years he returned to his roots. He visited Moldovița with family members in 2000 and again in 2008, prepared “for the coming generations of our family” the presentation “The Rosner–Wassermann Family”, wrote his memoirs, and in 2009 gave testimony to Yad Vashem. He died on 13 August 2016 in Kfar Yona, and left behind three sons and nine grandchildren.
story.maccabi.title: Maccabi Moldovița versus Maccabi Câmpulung
story.maccabi.summary: A childhood story about the village football team, Schmoll balls, and the match that inaugurated the “stadium” against Maccabi Câmpulung.
story.maccabi.long: As a boy in Moldovița, Yitzhak played for Maccabi Moldovița. The story tells how the children collected Schmoll shoe-polish tokens to get footballs, how a pitch was set up with the priest’s permission, and how the inaugural match against Maccabi Câmpulung ended when he scored an own goal in the 85th minute.

story.leo.long: Yitzhak writes about the house in Moldovița and about two boys who boarded with the family, David Berl and Leo Schnap, and he recounts Leo’s later fate, including his arrest as a “communist”.

story.conversation.long: A family conversation, transcribed, in which Yitzhak describes the walk to Shargorod in November 1941, the room at Sonia Starkman’s where four people lived, fetching water from a spring, forced labor at the gendarmerie, hunger and typhus, the liberation, the journey to Czernowitz and the escape to Botoșani, and his work as an interpreter.

tl.e07.text: Together with all the Jews of Gura Humorului the family was deported to Transnistria. After about two weeks of a “road of suffering” they reached Shargorod. A certificate from the Moldovița municipality from 1948 attests that he was deported with his parents in October 1941.

tl.e08.title: The Shargorod ghetto
tl.e08.text: Four family members lived in one room in the house of Sonia Starkman. He brought water from a spring about three kilometres away, and three days a week he peeled potatoes in the gendarmerie kitchen. In the ghetto an old doctor from the family also taught him grammar, physics and German stenography. And in the family: Yitzhak (Isaak) Sherf, who was among the heads of the Jewish council in the ghetto alongside Meir Teich, belonged to the Sherf family related to ours; one of his sons later held a senior role in Israel’s first government (family confirmation, 9.11.2026).

tl.e09.title: Liberation by the Red Army
tl.e09.text: A Russian officer climbed onto a tank and spoke in Yiddish: “You are free.” After about a month the family left on foot with the Wassermann family for Czernowitz, and from there fled to Botoșani. There are three versions of the date of liberation: in the written story it is said that the family remained in Shargorod until the end of May 1944; in the 2009 testimony (part 2, 03:52) Yitzhak said the liberation was on 21 March, “exactly on the first day of spring”; according to the historical sources Shargorod was liberated on 20 March 1944.

tl.e10.title: Interpreter with the Second Ukrainian Front
tl.e10.text: In Botoșani he was taken on as an interpreter at the Russian headquarters that administered the Romanian territory. He had taught himself Russian, with a grammar and a Russian–German dictionary. An official certificate from 1946 attests to the service. The archive also holds a Russian certificate (“spravka”) of 13.9.1944 from military unit 25837, stating that “Rozner Jacques” works with the unit as an interpreter.

ctx.c01.title: Bukovina is annexed to Austria
ctx.c01.text: The Habsburg army captured north-western Moldavia in 1774, and in 1775 the area was formally annexed as “Bukovina”. The first census recorded 526 Jewish families there.
ctx.c02.title: Bukovina becomes a crown land
ctx.c02.text: The March Constitution of 1849 separated Bukovina from Galicia and made it an autonomous crown land whose capital was Czernowitz.
ctx.c03.title: The Romanian constitution denies Jews citizenship
ctx.c03.text: Article 7 of Romania’s constitution restricted citizenship to Christians. Between 1880 and 1913 only 529 Jews received citizenship.
ctx.c04.title: The emancipation of Austrian Jews
ctx.c04.text: The Jews of the Habsburg Empire, including the Jews of Bukovina, received full equality of rights. The number of Jews in Bukovina rose from 14,581 in 1850 to 102,919 in 1910.
ctx.c05.title: Yiddish theatre is born in Iași
ctx.c05.text: Abraham Goldfaden staged in Iași the first production of the Yiddish theatre. In 1899 Jews made up more than half the city’s residents.
ctx.c06.title: The First World War in Bukovina
ctx.c06.text: The Russian army occupied Bukovina, and many Jewish families fled. In 1916 the Russians dismantled the sawmills of Moldovița.
ctx.c07.title: Bukovina is annexed to Romania
ctx.c07.text: The Romanian army entered Bukovina, and the province was joined to Greater Romania and lost its autonomy.
ctx.c08.title: The Romanian constitution grants rights to Jews
ctx.c08.text: Following the minority treaties of 1919, the constitution of 1923 anchored the civil rights of Romanian Jews. In the same year A. C. Cuza’s antisemitic league was founded.
ctx.c09.title: The Goga–Cuza government
ctx.c09.text: An antisemitic government headed by Octavian Goga came to power and enacted decrees against the Jews. It fell after about 40 days.
ctx.c10.title: “The review of citizenship”
ctx.c10.text: Decree-law no. 169 required Jews to prove their citizenship anew. By the end of the process citizenship was stripped from 225,222 Jews.
ctx.c11.title: Northern Bukovina passes to the Soviet Union
ctx.c11.text: Following a Soviet ultimatum, Romania gave up Bessarabia and northern Bukovina. The retreating army maltreated Jews.
ctx.c12.title: The Romanian racial laws
ctx.c12.text: Decree-law 2650 defined Jews by “blood” and forbade them, among other things, to hold rural property and to engage in the village economy.
ctx.c13.title: Antonescu and the Iron Guard in power
ctx.c13.text: Ion Antonescu and the Iron Guard proclaimed the “National Legionary State”. In October–December 1940 Jews were expelled from dozens of villages to the county towns.
ctx.c14.title: A Yom Kippur of terror in Câmpulung
ctx.c14.text: Legionaries, policemen and soldiers looted Jewish homes in Câmpulung, the county town of Moldovița, and abused Rabbi Yosef Rubin.
ctx.c15.title: The Legionary rebellion and the Bucharest pogrom
ctx.c15.text: The Iron Guard rebelled against Antonescu, and during the rebellion dozens of Jews were murdered in Bucharest.
ctx.c16.title: The Iași pogrom
ctx.c16.text: In the city of Yitzhak’s birth thousands of Jews were murdered in the streets and in the police courtyard, and thousands more died on the “death trains”. Estimates range from more than 8,000 to more than 10,000 murdered.
ctx.c17.title: The Tighina agreement: Transnistria
ctx.c17.text: Germany handed Romania the territory between the Dniester and the Bug, “Transnistria”, to administer.
ctx.c18.title: The beginning of the deportation from southern Bukovina
ctx.c18.text: The deportation of the Jews of southern Bukovina to Transnistria began, first from Suceava. Estimates are that between about 21,000 and more than 26,000 Jews were deported.
ctx.c18.src.0: The “Elie Wiesel” National Institute for the Study of the Holocaust in Romania
ctx.c19.title: The deportation of the Jews of Gura Humorului
ctx.c19.text: 2,954 Jews from Gura Humorului and the surrounding villages were deported in a single day to Transnistria, via Ataki and the Dniester.
ctx.c20.title: The Shargorod ghetto fills with deportees
ctx.c20.text: Thousands of deportees, most of them from Bukovina, joined the roughly 1,800 Jews of Shargorod. In November 1941 a Jewish council headed by Meir Teich was established. And in the family: Yitzhak (Isaak) Sherf, who was among the heads of the Jewish council in the ghetto alongside Meir Teich, belonged to the Sherf family related to ours; one of his sons later held a senior role in Israel’s first government (family confirmation, 9.11.2026).
ctx.c20.src.0: Yad Vashem – the Encyclopaedia of the Ghettos
ctx.c21.title: The typhus epidemic in Shargorod
ctx.c21.text: Of about 9,000 Jews in Shargorod, 2,414 fell ill with typhus, and 1,449 of them died. In February 1942 a 100-bed hospital was opened in the ghetto.
ctx.c22.title: The deportations are halted
ctx.c22.text: The Romanian government halted the deportations to Transnistria and refused the German plan to send Romania’s Jews to Bełżec.
ctx.c23.title: Antonescu permits the return of the deportees
ctx.c23.text: As the Soviet army advanced, Antonescu agreed to the return of the deportees to Romania.
ctx.c24.title: The liberation of Shargorod
ctx.c24.text: The Red Army liberated Shargorod and the Jews of the ghetto. This is the date in the historical sources. In Yitzhak’s written story it is said that the family remained until the end of May 1944, and in the 2009 testimony he said the liberation was on 21 March.
ctx.c24.src.0: Yad Vashem – the Encyclopaedia of the Ghettos
ctx.c25.title: A coup in Romania
ctx.c25.text: King Michael deposed Antonescu, and Romania signed an armistice with the Soviet Union and went over to the side of the Allies.
ctx.c26.title: A first aliyah from Gura Humorului
ctx.c26.text: 140 of the Jews of Gura Humorului left for the Land of Israel via Cyprus. In the years 1948–1951 almost all of the city’s Jews left.
ctx.c26.src.0: JewishGen – the Gura Humorului yizkor book
ctx.c27.title: The liquidation of the Zionist movement in Romania
ctx.c27.text: The communist Interior Ministry ordered the liquidation of what remained of the Zionist movement, including the youth movements and the training farms.
ctx.c28.title: Immigration is frozen
ctx.c28.text: Romania almost completely halted the departure of Jews, and at the same time an anti-Zionist campaign was under way.
ctx.c29.title: About 100,000 Jews remained in Romania
ctx.c29.text: Following the waves of emigration, about 100,000 Jews remained in Romania in 1965. From the establishment of the state until the end of the 1960s more than 200,000 Jews made aliyah to Israel from Romania.
ctx.c30.title: Romania does not break off relations with Israel
ctx.c30.text: After the Six-Day War, Romania was the only country in the Eastern Bloc that did not break off its relations with Israel.
history.b13: Bukovina, “the land of beeches”, was part of the Principality of Moldavia. In 1774 the Austrian army captured it, and in 1775 it was formally annexed to the Habsburg monarchy. In the years 1786–1849 it was joined to Galicia, and from 1849 it was an autonomous crown land whose capital was Czernowitz. In the first Austrian census, in 1775, 526 Jewish families were recorded there. The authorities at first tried to restrict Jewish immigration, and even expelled new immigrants, but the number of Jews grew steadily: 14,581 in 1850 (3.8% of the population), 67,418 in 1880 and 102,919 in 1910 (12.9%).

history.b19: The full equality that Austrian Jews received in 1867 opened an era of growth for the Jews of Bukovina. According to Encyclopaedia Judaica, Jews initiated the timber and malt industries in Bukovina, and were prominent in the laying of railways and in banking. In 1906 Jews paid almost half of the district’s taxes. Many of them spoke German and sent their children to German schools. Alongside this, Hasidism remained strong, especially the Hasidic courts of Sadigura, Vizhnitz and Boyan. Zionism reached the province at the end of the 19th century, and Bukovina sent three delegates to the First Zionist Congress in 1897.
history.b20: Trees and rivers in southern Bukovina. In the southern towns, where the family’s life unfolded, the forest industry was the centre of livelihood. In Gura Humorului Jews settled in earnest only from 1835. At first they worked as craftsmen, merchants and suppliers to the Austrian army, and later they established woodworking workshops and sawmills. The community numbered 190 souls in 1867 and 2,050 in 1910. In Vatra Dornei the early Jewish presence is tied to the founding of the first sawmills, that is, to the beginnings of the forest industry. In Câmpulung (Câmpulung Moldovenesc) an independent community was established in 1859, and on the eve of the First World War about 3,500 Jews lived in the town and the surrounding villages. In Moldovița itself, then called Rușii-Moldoviței, sawmills were in operation. A report from 1916, quoted in a Romanian study, describes there “a large factory with twelve saws”, and in 1897 a wood-distillation plant was also established in the village. The Jewish cemetery of Moldovița, whose gravestones are inscribed in Hebrew and German, dates from the 19th century.
history.b21: And in the family: Yitzhak’s grandfather, Yitzhak Rosner the elder, was born according to the Geni record in 1850 in Putyla in northern Bukovina, and his father Litman was born in 1886 in Kisalitsa, “in the Austro-Hungarian Empire”, as Yitzhak wrote in the family presentation. Grandmother Chaya Sherf-Rosner was buried in Moldovița (the family tree on Geni).

history.b23: Iași, the capital of the Principality of Moldavia, was one of the important Jewish centres in Romania. In 1859 Jews were 47.1% of the city’s residents, and in 1899 they numbered 39,441 souls, more than half the population. In 1876 Abraham Goldfaden’s first Yiddish theatre performance took place in Iași, and the city became a centre of Yiddish literature. On the other hand, the University of Iași was a focus of antisemitism. The economist Alexandru C. Cuza taught there, and in 1923 the “League of National-Christian Defence” headed by Cuza was founded. In 1930, 35,465 Jews lived in the city (34.4%).
history.b24: The Great Synagogue in Iași (photograph 2002)Avishai Teicher · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
history.b25: In the Old Kingdom of Romania (the “Regat”), citizenship was withheld from most Jews throughout the 19th century. Article 7 of the 1866 constitution reserved citizenship for Christians alone. Between 1880 and 1913 only 529 Jews received citizenship, and only the minority treaties of 1919 and the constitution of 1923 granted the Jews of Romania full civil rights.
history.b26: And in the family: Yitzhak was born in Iași on 25 November 1926, according to his Israeli documents. His mother, Regina Markovitz, was born in 1898 in Burdujeni near Suceava.
history.b27: Sources: YIVO – Iași · YIVO – Romania · Jewish Virtual Library – Romania
history.b28: In the First World War the Russian army invaded Bukovina and occupied it, and many Jewish families fled for fear of persecution. A Romanian study describes how in 1916 the Russians dismantled the sawmills of Moldovița and sent the machinery to Russia. In November 1918 the Romanian army entered Bukovina, and the province was annexed to Romania, a step confirmed by the Treaty of Saint-Germain. The Jewish representatives remained neutral and did not support the union. Within Romania, Bukovina lost its autonomy and was divided into counties, including Câmpulung county, to which Moldovița belonged (as also appears in the heading of the Moldovița municipal certificate of 1948). In 1930, 92,232 Jews lived in Bukovina (10.8%). They were recognised as a national minority, but were gradually worn down under a policy of “Romanianisation” and growing antisemitism.

history.b30: And in the family: Litman was conscripted in 1912 into the Austrian army, and in 1916 he fell into Russian captivity. When he was returned in 1918, “Bukovina, his homeland, was no longer in Austria but in Romania”. In Vienna he met Regina, “a young refugee from Bukovina”. They married in 1922, and in 1923 they returned to settle in Moldovița near his sister Fanny Wassermann (from Yitzhak’s notes in the family presentation “RW Family”).
history.b31: Sources: YIVO – Bucovina · YIVO – Romania · Analele Bucovinei 2024 (PDF)
history.b32: In the 1930s the extreme right grew stronger in Romania. The fascist “Iron Guard” (the “Legion”) won broad popular support, and beside it operated the National-Christian Party of Octavian Goga and Alexandru C. Cuza. In December 1937 Goga formed a government, and it immediately began to legislate against the Jews. The most important of the laws was decree-law no. 169 of January 1938, “the review of citizenship”: every Jew was required to prove anew, within 40 days, his right to citizenship. The Goga government fell after about 40 days, among other reasons following an economic boycott by the Jews and international pressure, but the law remained in force under the royal dictatorship of Carol II. By the end of the process citizenship was stripped from 225,222 Jews, that is from 73,253 families. In effect the law cancelled the citizenship given to Jews since the First World War, and therefore it also struck the Jews of Bukovina, who had become Romanian citizens only after 1918.
history.b33: The Great Synagogue in Vatra Dornei, 1936Anonymous · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
history.b34: And in the family: In these years Yitzhak grew up as a child in Moldovița. He wrote about the players of “Maccabi Moldovița” and about the match against “Maccabi Câmpulung” in the summer of 1937 (Maccabi Moldovița versus Maccabi Câmpulung), and about the house and about Leo Schnap, who was arrested as a “communist” (Who am I? And Leo Schnap).
history.b35: Sources: The final report of the International Commission on the Holocaust in Romania (the Wiesel Commission), chapter 1 (PDF) · Yad Vashem – Bukovina (Hebrew, PDF) · YIVO – Romania · USHMM – Romania · Jewish Virtual Library – Romania
history.b36: On 26 June 1940 the Soviet Union demanded Bessarabia and northern Bukovina, and on 28 June Romania yielded. Czernowitz passed under Soviet rule, and Bukovina was split in two. The retreating Romanian army accused the Jews of sympathy for communism, and dozens of Jews were murdered along the way. In northern Bukovina the Soviets deported in June 1941 about 3,800 to 4,000 Jews to Siberia, as “bourgeois” and “enemies of the people”.
history.b37: The old synagogue in Câmpulung (Câmpulung Moldovenesc) (photograph 2011)Cezar Suceveanu · CC BY-SA 3.0 (license) · Wikimedia Commons · The image was reduced for the site; the reduced version is distributed under the same licence
history.b38: On 9 August 1940 the Gigurtu government published decree-law no. 2650, which defined Jews by “blood” and was inspired by the Nuremberg Laws. The decree removed Jews from public posts and from many professions, and forbade them to hold rural property or to engage in economic activity in villages. In September 1940 General Ion Antonescu came to power together with the Iron Guard, and the “National Legionary State” was proclaimed. From October to December 1940 the Legion’s commanders expelled Jews from dozens of villages where they had lived for more than a hundred years, and turned them into refugees in the county towns. On Yom Kippur, 12 October 1940, a “day of terror” took place in Câmpulung: soldiers, policemen and legionaries looted Jewish homes, and Rabbi Yosef Rubin was tortured, humiliated and harnessed to a cart. The Romanianisation laws ultimately expropriated from Jews, among other things, 47,455 hectares of forests.
history.b39: And in the family: Yitzhak wrote that “in the summer of 1940… a law was enacted according to which Jews were forbidden to live in villages”. The family was given three days to leave Moldovița, the house was locked and sealed in the presence of two policemen of the Legionary police, and they moved to Gura Humorului, to relatives of his mother from the Ellenbogen family. Litman’s timber business, which until then had exported mainly to Britain and the Land of Israel, was required to export to Germany (Shargorod – the first chapter).
history.b40: Sources: The Wiesel Commission – executive summary (PDF) · The Wiesel Commission, chapter 1 – decree-law 2650 (PDF) · The Wiesel Commission, chapter 5 – the expulsion of village Jews and the terror in Câmpulung (PDF) · YIVO – Câmpulung Moldovenesc · Yad Vashem – Bukovina (Hebrew, PDF) · USHMM – Romania
history.b41: In January 1941 the Iron Guard rebelled against Antonescu, and during the rebellion the legionaries carried out a murderous pogrom against the Jews of Bucharest. On 22 June 1941 Romania joined the German invasion of the Soviet Union. Already on 28 June there began in Iași, the city of Yitzhak’s birth, a pogrom planned by the state authorities. Romanian and German soldiers, policemen and residents murdered Jews in homes and in the streets, and on 29 June, “Black Sunday”, thousands were shot in the courtyard of police headquarters. About 4,300 survivors were crammed into the “death trains”, and there about 2,600 died of thirst and suffocation. There is no agreement on the number of those murdered: the Holocaust Museum in Washington writes “at least 4,000” in the city itself; according to Yad Vashem the police reported to Antonescu more than 8,000, and the court in 1948 determined that more than 10,000 were murdered; YIVO estimates about 14,000 victims, including the trains.
history.b42: The “death train” from Iași, July 1941 (a historically difficult photograph)An unknown journalist · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
history.b43: In northern Bukovina, which was recaptured, about 15,000 Jews were murdered in July 1941. On 18 June 1941 Antonescu ordered that the Jews of the villages and small towns be concentrated in the county towns.
history.b44: Sources: Yad Vashem – the Iași pogrom, June 1941 · Yad Vashem – a lesson plan on the Iași pogrom · USHMM – Romania · YIVO – Iași · Yad Vashem – Bukovina (Hebrew, PDF)
history.b45: The Jews of southern Bukovina were not deported because of any offence. They had never lived under Soviet rule. The Wiesel Commission determined that the deportation was the result of a decision by the two Antonescus, Ion and Mihai, on “ethnic cleansing”, as documented in the minutes of government meetings of 25 June and 6 October 1941. The deportation began on 9 October 1941 in Suceava, and on 10 October a train left Gura Humorului. According to Encyclopaedia Judaica, 2,954 Jews were deported from Gura Humorului in a single day, residents of the town and refugees from the surrounding villages. The memorial plaque in the town synagogue mentions about 3,000 deportees on 10 and 11 October. From Câmpulung the transports left on 12 and 13 October, and only 28 “essential” Jews were allowed to remain. From Vatra Dornei everyone was deported, except 21 souls. The Wiesel Commission estimates the number of deportees from southern Bukovina in 1941–1942 at 21,229, and the “Elie Wiesel” Institute writes of “more than 26,000”.
history.b46: The Great Synagogue in Gura Humorului (photograph 2010)Cezar Suceveanu · CC BY 3.0 (license) · Wikimedia Commons
history.b47: The Dniester and Mohyliv-Podilskyi (Mogilev), the crossing point of the deportees, a view from the bridge (2015)Gikü · CC0 (license) · Wikimedia Commons
history.b48: The trains arrived at Atachi, on the western bank of the Dniester. There the deportees were robbed by officials of the national bank, gendarmes and soldiers. They crossed the river on rafts or on a pontoon bridge to Mogilev (Mohyliv-Podilskyi), and some of them drowned. From Mogilev they were sent in convoys to the ghettos of Shargorod, Kopaygorod, Murafa and Djurin. The identity papers of many of them were burned at the crossing points, so that they would arrive in Transnistria without identity.
history.b49: And in the family: According to his memoirs, on 8 October 1941 all the Jews of Gura Humorului were ordered to report the next day, 9 October at 10:00, at the railway station, each with a single bundle. His mother, Gina, sewed into her coat 220,000 lei that his father had prepared in advance. The text he wrote breaks off at the moment of waiting for the train (Shargorod · Shargorod, English). A certificate from the Moldovița municipality from 1948 attests that he was deported with his parents to Transnistria in October 1941 (the document).
history.b50: A discrepancy in the date of the deportation: In the diary and in the story he wrote (“Shargorod”) it is said that the assembly at the station was on 9 October 1941, whereas according to the historical sources (JBAT, Encyclopaedia Judaica and the memorial plaque in the synagogue) the train from Gura Humorului left on 10 October 1941. In the testimony to Yad Vashem (2009) he said: “On the ninth of October we received an order… on the tenth of October to come” (part 1, 56:02). The exact date has not yet been settled.

history.b52: “Transnistria”, that is “beyond the Dniester”, was the name Romania gave to the territory between the Dniester and the Bug. Hitler handed it to Romania, and according to the Tighina agreement of 30 August 1941 it was administered by Romania. The deportees from Bukovina and Bessarabia were concentrated in ghettos and camps without food, without housing and without medical care, and they were subject to forced labour. The winter of 1941/42 was the hardest of all, and tens of thousands died of hunger, cold, typhus and dysentery. Of about 145,000 to 150,000 deportees from Romania, about 90,000 perished. The Holocaust Museum in Washington estimates that in Transnistria altogether 280,000 to 380,000 Jews were murdered, and many of them were local Jews from Ukraine.

history.b56: Shargorod. Shargorod (today Sharhorod in Ukraine) was a long-established Jewish town, with a splendid fortified synagogue. The Germans captured it on 22 July 1941, and in September it was attached to Transnistria, to Mogilev county. On the eve of the war about 1,660 Jews lived there. In the autumn of 1941 thousands of deportees arrived: according to Yad Vashem about 3,000 at the beginning of October, and according to Encyclopaedia Judaica about 5,000 in October and November. Most of them were from Bukovina, and especially from Suceava. In November 1941 a joint Jewish council was established, headed by Meir Teich of Suceava. The council organised a public kitchen that distributed 1,500 meals a day, disinfection ovens, a bathhouse, a 100-bed hospital (in February 1942), a soap factory, a pharmacy and an orphanage for 600 children. According to the Wiesel Commission, 2,414 of about 9,000 Jews in Shargorod fell ill with typhus, and 1,449 of them died. Other estimates range from about 1,400 (Yad Vashem) to 4,000 (the historian Jean Ancel). About half of the doctors in the ghetto themselves died. On 30 June 1942 about a thousand Jews were dispersed to the surrounding villages. In September 1943, 2,731 Jews from Bukovina and 240 from Bessarabia remained in the ghetto.
history.b57: And in the family: In a recorded family conversation Yitzhak described the walk to Shargorod in November 1941, the room at Sonia Starkman’s where four people lived, the water they carried from a spring about three kilometres away, the forced labour at the gendarmerie, the hunger and the typhus (A conversation about Shargorod). He also sketched the apartment in the ghetto and marked on a map the houses of the Wassermann, Rosner and Zimmerman families. In 2013 he wrote a short passage about a friend who grew thinner and thinner until one Sabbath he was no longer there (The friend who vanished). Yitzhak (Isaak) Sherf, who was among the heads of the Jewish council in the ghetto alongside Meir Teich (Nationalities Papers), belonged to the Sherf family related to ours; one of his sons later held a senior role in Israel’s first government (family confirmation, 9.11.2026).
history.b58: Sources: Yad Vashem – the Encyclopaedia of the Ghettos: Shargorod (Hebrew) · Yad Vashem – Transnistria (Hebrew, PDF) · Encyclopaedia Judaica / JVL – Shargorod · The Wiesel Commission, chapter 5 (PDF) · Nationalities Papers – Institutions for survival: The Shargorod ghetto · USHMM – Transnistria Governorate · YIVO – Transnistria
history.b59: As the Red Army drew nearer, the Romanian authorities permitted a partial return. In December 1943 the survivors of Dorohoi were returned, and in March 1944 orphans. Only on 14 March 1944 did Antonescu agree to the return of all the deportees, but the decision came too late, and in the second half of March 1944 only about 2,500 people were returned in an organised way. The Red Army liberated Shargorod on 20 March 1944. On 23 August 1944 King Michael deposed Antonescu, and Romania signed an armistice with the Soviet Union. Antonescu was executed in 1946. In Shargorod itself the Soviets arrested in 1944 the heads of the Jewish council, including Meir Teich, and put them on trial for “collaboration”. The armistice agreement and the peace treaty of 1947 re-established the 1940 border, so that northern Bukovina remained in the Soviet Union. Many deportees from southern Bukovina returned to their towns at the end of 1944 and the beginning of 1945, and most of them left a few years later and made aliyah to Israel.

history.b61: And in the family: On the date of the liberation and the departure from Shargorod there are different versions: in the written story it is said that the family remained there until the end of May 1944; in the 2009 testimony (part 2, 03:52) Yitzhak said the liberation was on 21 March, “exactly on the first day of spring”; according to the historical sources Shargorod was liberated on 20 March 1944. The exact date of the family’s departure is not known. From there they set out for Czernowitz with the Wassermann family, were robbed on the way, and Yitzhak fled conscription for labour in the mines and reached Botoșani. An official certificate from 1946 attests that between 15 July and 15 October 1944 he served as an interpreter in the “special command of the Second Ukrainian Front” of the Red Army (the document). According to the municipal certificate, he and his parents returned to Moldovița in May 1945 (the document).
history.b62: Sources: The Wiesel Commission – executive summary (PDF) · YIVO – Transnistria · Yad Vashem – the Encyclopaedia of the Ghettos: Shargorod · USHMM – Romania · Journal of Modern European History – the trials of the Shargorod ghetto council · YIVO – Bucovina · Yad Vashem – Bukovina (Hebrew, PDF)
history.b63: At the end of the war there lived in Romania, according to various estimates, between about 350,000 (according to Ioanid) and about 430,000 (according to YIVO) Jews. This was the largest Jewish community remaining in Europe outside the Soviet Union. In the years 1944–1947, 14 immigrant ships left Romanian ports with about 24,000 olim. From Gura Humorului a first group of 140 olim left in September 1947 via Cyprus, and in the years 1948–1951 almost all of the city’s Jews left. The communist regime dismantled the Zionist movement in 1948–1949 and nationalised the Jewish schools, and between April 1952 and 1956 it almost completely halted emigration. From the establishment of the state until the end of the 1960s more than 200,000 Jews made aliyah to Israel from Romania, and in 1965 about 100,000 remained there. Behind the scenes, as the historian Radu Ioanid described, Israel “bought” exit visas: in the 1950s and 1960s in barter deals of agricultural and industrial equipment, and from 1969 for cash. In 1967 Romania was the only country in the Eastern Bloc that did not break off its relations with Israel.
history.b64: And in the family: In 1945 Yitzhak studied at the polytechnic in Bucharest and worked delivering newspapers, and then he first met his cousin Bibi Rosner-Boico (The meeting with Bibi). In the 1950s he was a young officer in Bucharest (A morning walk to work). In February 1968 he received, in the name of “Adrian Roșca”, a Romanian travel document “for persons without citizenship” (the document). He passed through Vienna and landed at Lod on 15 May 1968, and on 4 August 1968 he officially changed his name to Yitzhak Rosner.

tl.e42.title: Baccalaureate diploma
tl.e42.text: In the September 1946 session in Bucharest he passed the theoretical baccalaureate as a graduate of the “Cultura A” lyceum, with an average of 6.20, ranked 22nd of 164 successful candidates. The diploma was issued on 10 March 1947. According to the grade sheet he studied in 9th grade (1939/40) at the Dragoș Vodă lyceum, in 10th grade (1942/43) at the A. Pumnul lyceum, and in 11th–12th grades (1944/45) at Cultura A. In his 1991 letter he wrote that he completed secondary school in evening courses and passed the Abitur in March 1947.
tl.e43.title: Working at the newspaper “România Liberă”
tl.e43.text: In a German letter of 14.12.1991 he wrote that from October 1944 to November 1948 he worked in the printing and distribution of the newspaper România Liberă. In the first two years he was mostly an office trainee, and because of the great post-war paper shortage he travelled 2–3 times a week from Bucharest to the paper mill in Bușteni (about 120 km) to obtain the paper needed.
tl.e44.note: The 2009 testimony and the letter “Meeting Boico” describe studies at the Polytechnic from autumn 1945 (see the “Autumn 1945” event); the 1991 letter says the studies began in September 1947.
tl.e44.title: Electrical and radio engineering studies, and work before dawn
tl.e44.text: According to the 1991 letter, in September 1947 he began studying electrical and radio engineering and moved to the newspaper’s dispatch department: he worked from 4 a.m. to noon, Tuesday to Sunday, and studied on Monday mornings and every day from 3 to 8 p.m. At the end of the year he could not pass all the exams, because he had been unable to attend the morning classes. At the end of 1948 he left the job to devote himself to his studies, but again and again had to find work to make a living.
tl.e45.title: Radio technician and technical officer
tl.e45.text: According to the 1991 letter, in 1949 he was offered the chance to interrupt his studies and take a post as a radio technician at a state office, and he accepted at once. He was trained as a technical officer in a six-week course, and his studies were interrupted and never completed.
tl.e46.title: Forced to leave a senior post (according to the family album)
tl.e46.text: The family album says: “In the 1950s the Romanians decided / they were a bit fed up with the Jews – / Yitzhak, as his bad luck would have it, / had to part with a senior post. / Imagine him sitting idle – / better by now to make aliyah to Israel!”

tl.e47.title: ELECTRONICA: a television assembly line with a French team
tl.e47.text: According to the 1991 letter, at the ELECTRONICA factory, whose general director had been one of his teachers at the vocational school, he was registered as a worker but worked in the plant’s technical management. In the summer of 1960 he worked with a French team setting up an assembly line for television sets, and after the French left he remained responsible for the department’s production technology.
tl.e48.title: Television technician in a repair laboratory
tl.e48.text: According to the 1991 letter, his salary at the factory was low, because he was not paid according to his actual work, so in 1963 he left and began working as a television technician in a repair laboratory, where he earned much more. He stayed in this job until he emigrated to Israel in 1968.
tl.e49.title: Translator’s certificate from German
tl.e49.text: The Romanian Ministry of Education and Culture awarded “Rosca Adrian” translator’s certificate No. 317, German to Romanian, specialty fiction, on the basis of an examination in the October 1960 session. He left Romania in 1968 under the name Adrian Roșca, and the name-change certificate of 4.8.1968 changed it to Yitzhak Rosner.
tl.e50.title: Translator’s certificate from French and English
tl.e50.text: Translator’s certificate No. 01586 from the State Committee for Culture and Art, on the basis of an examination in the April 1967 session: French to Romanian, specialty electronics, and English to Romanian, specialty geography.
tl.e22.title: Abu Rudeis: head of the electrical department, and meeting Ruth
tl.e22.text: From 23.8.1970 to 30.11.1975 he worked for Netivei Neft as head of the electrical department at the Abu Rudeis oil field in Sinai: design of low- and medium-voltage installations (2.4 and 10.5 kV) and control systems, operation and maintenance of three power stations totalling 6.5 MW, a 25 km distribution network, and management of a team of 40 skilled workers. There he met Ruth. In the story “A morning walk to work” he wrote that he offered a ride to a young woman who had newly arrived at the field, and “on the spot I made a fateful decision: this is the woman I want to wake up next to in the morning.” The family album says: “on a fine summer morning, August ’72, / on the way to work / he meets me – a fairly young woman. / Three months of a stormy romance / and we decided to give up being single.”

tl.e41.title: Marriage to Ruth
tl.e41.text: Yitzhak and Ruth were married in Tel Aviv–Jaffa on the eve of Friday, 11 Nisan 5733 (12.4.1973). On the marriage certificate Yitzhak is listed as an electrical engineer and Ruth as a chemical engineer. Congratulatory telegrams arrived at the Chief Rabbinate halls in Tel Aviv, among them from Meir Giron and from Eitan Eisenberg, manager of Netivei Neft. According to the family, Eisenberg at first did not want to hire Ruth because she was a woman, and hired her after an interview with him.

tl.e51.title: The Yom Kippur War at Abu Rudeis
tl.e51.text: The family album says: “Another half year passed / and the Yom Kippur War broke out. / Yitzhak guards installations at ‘Abu Rudeis’, / and I am in Tel Aviv with a growing belly, / present every morning at ‘Netivei Neft’.” On 23.10.1973 the field manager, Haim Zucker, wrote him a letter of thanks: “I turn to you with an expression of thanks and appreciation from the heart”; “together we went through a hard time: a strike on the field, a clash, bombing, constant readiness, guard duty at the lookout.” He added: “the time has not yet come to rest on our laurels; the hour has come to rehabilitate the field.”

tl.e53.title: A letter to Ruth
tl.e53.text: A letter in German from Yitzhak to Ruth while she was pregnant: “There are so many things I would like to write or talk to you about that I don’t know where to begin.” He writes about missing her, about how at the last moment she was not allowed to come to him, about the fight over her job – “the law does not allow pregnant women to be dismissed” – and about salary differences, and ends: “the main thing is that I love you very, very much and that you shouldn’t fret but always think only of all 3 of us.”
tl.e23.title: Sharon and Eylon are born
tl.e23.text: The family album says: “When the fighting ends he comes home, / he will not miss Sharon’s birth, / and so in March ’74, after a working day, / Sharon is born – a wonderful baby. / In March ’75 Eylon too hurries to arrive – / the whole family is full of joy and gladness.” According to Geni, both were born in Tel Aviv.

tl.e54.text: According to the Netivei Neft reference, Yitzhak “fulfilled his duties to the complete satisfaction of the management of the oil field” and finished his employment “due to the end of our operation in the Abu Rudeis”.

tl.e58.text: The Ministry of the Interior in Tel Aviv issued a citizenship certificate (under the Citizenship Law, 1952) in Hebrew and German: Rosner Yitzhak / ROSNER YIZHAK, born in Iași, is an Israeli citizen.

tl.e55.title: Peace with Egypt, the fire, and a hard time
tl.e55.text: The family album says: “Sadat comes to the capital, / a peace treaty is signed – and Sinai was returned. / Meanwhile there is also a big fire, / and Yitzhak is left without a livelihood – a hard time, / but somehow the family manages to get by.”

tl.e56.title: Moving house, and the home with the yard (according to the family album)
tl.e56.text: The family album describes the family’s moves: “The Rosners, with their Romanian past, / now take on a gypsy hue” – Or Yehuda, the Har Aviv guesthouse, Shtand Street in Tel Aviv, “one lane and another lane in Be’er Sheva”, “a kibbutz for a change” and an address on HaTzvi Street. “But everywhere there is joy / and the family spends time together.” And on the next page: “after talks and arguments” they moved from HaTzvi Street to Kikar HaGanim, “and so we found a neglected yard / that after a year was in bloom.”

album.02.title: “Dr Jacques” – childhood
album.02.text:
In a town in northern Romania
“Dr Jacques” was born, the wonderful prince –
a small family, a big sister,
a sweet father with a dignified bald head
and the mother – a strong woman.

In a charming landscape, with cows and horses,
the family lived a good life in the Diaspora
until… the Germans and the Romanians
decide to deport them together with others.

… There are of course periods
of which there are no photos.
So – it is good to have a friend
who can tell a little…
album.07.title: After the war – to the city
album.07.text:
The war ends,
and the family returns,
but the young man
has dreams – he sets out for the city.

His charm works on Russians and Romanians,
leftists and rightists –
and he advances thanks to his many talents.

The young man studies and also starts a family,
he has a mischievous son named Dani.
A number of years have passed
and here is Dani at 20.
Perhaps Dani will tell of some of his deeds?!
album.08.title: The 1950s
album.08.text:
In the 1950s the Romanians decided
they were a bit fed up with the Jews –
Yitzhak, as his bad luck would have it,
had to part with a senior post.
Imagine him sitting idle –
better by now to make aliyah to Israel!
album.09.title: 1968 – aliyah
album.09.text:
The parents and the sister received a visa to emigrate
and Yitzhak was left behind, despite 7–8 applications.

Overseas, family and friends
keep helping and finally succeed
with money and also connections.
And so in ’68 the small Rosner family
arrived in Haifa.
Here a corner is kept for Yitzhak and for others.
In Israel he does not find his beloved sister,
but elderly parents and a sweet nephew await him eagerly.
album.p10.title: Canada, Sinai and Ruth
album.p10.text:
His friend Rubin offers help
and Jacques tries his luck in Canada.
After a few months the “dandy” returns
and decides to bet on Sinai now.

So it happened, and on a fine summer morning, August ’72,
on the way to work
he meets me – a fairly young woman.
Three months of a stormy romance
and we decided to give up being single.
album.p11.title: The Yom Kippur War
album.p11.text:
Another half year passed
and the Yom Kippur War broke out.
Yitzhak guards installations at “Abu Rudeis”,
and I am in Tel Aviv with a growing belly,
present every morning at “Netivei Neft”.
album.p12.title: Sharon and Eylon
album.p12.text:
When the fighting ends he comes home,
he will not miss Sharon’s birth,
and so in March ’74, after a working day,
Sharon is born – a wonderful baby.
In March ’75 Eylon too hurries to arrive –
the whole family is full of joy and gladness.
album.p13.title: Peace, Sinai and the fire
album.p13.text:
Sadat comes to the capital,
a peace treaty is signed – and Sinai was returned.
Meanwhile there is also a big fire,
and Yitzhak is left without a livelihood – a hard time,
but somehow the family manages to get by.
album.p14.title: On the move
album.p14.text:
The Rosners, with their Romanian past,
now take on a gypsy hue:
Or Yehuda, the Har Aviv guesthouse,
Shtand Street in Tel Aviv,
one lane and another lane in Be’er Sheva,
a kibbutz for a change
and after it another address on HaTzvi Street.
But everywhere there is joy
and the family spends time together.
There are children and grandchildren too,
there are friends like Tzipi and Moshe
who have accompanied us over the years.
album.p15.title: The house and the yard
album.p15.text:
After talks and arguments
we moved from HaTzvi Street to Kikar HaGanim.
And so we found a neglected yard
that after a year was in bloom.
album.p16.title: Trips, holidays and friends
album.p16.text:
I spoke about apartments,
but in that period there were other tasks too:
a first trip abroad, Saturday outings, holidays,
family events, parties and new friends:
with the Bar Yaakov family we grow older and raise children,
and the Spivaks join in too.
Meanwhile we also work hard, and cook.
We develop the garden, and also take in aliyah [new immigrants; the Hebrew can also be read “on it”].
From time to time we also travel – and not always on trips.
